# Inference, precision and ambiguity {#sec-phase-delay-inference}

A phase-sensitive receiver reports a nearly straight phase slope across frequency.
How precisely can we estimate delay, and does the fitted slope identify the delay
we actually want? These are different questions. A narrow statistical interval
can surround the wrong ambiguity branch or include an unknown receiver path.
We will derive a usable local estimator before testing its global interpretation.

The prerequisite chain is deliberate. [The phase comparison](phase-comparison.qmd)
fixes orientation and planes, [scalar stochastic phase](scalar-stochastic-phase.qmd)
separates records from ensembles and explains noise-to-phase assumptions,
[observation weighting](observation-weighted-coherence.qmd) defines the observation,
and [covariance](covariance-quadratic-forms.qmd) explains coupled errors and rank.
Keep their explicit local conventions: channel 2 relative to channel 1, positive
physical delay giving negative phase slope, and phase measured in radians. These
choices remain local. The calculation below is synthetic, not a measured receiver.

## Specify the observations and unknowns

At fixed input/output reference planes, measure a complex channel comparison at
N known swept physical RF frequencies f_i during one settled acquisition state.
The y_i below are comparisons translated to the physical input-phase orientation,
not arbitrary raw positive-IF angles. For the lower-side model in Chapter 1,
y=theta+Delta_lambda-Delta_beta; for its upper-side model,
y=-theta+Delta_lambda+Delta_beta. Known path terms are removed in that translation;
unknown receiver delay remains a nuisance contribution to the fitted total.
This step must follow the actual conversion topology before interpreting a slope. Assume the underlying
transfer has constant amplitude above a declared validity threshold and phase
linear in frequency over this band. Let f0 be the arithmetic mean of the frequencies
and x_i=f_i-f0, in Hz. On a justified unwrapped branch the observations are

$$
 y_i=a+b x_i+\epsilon_i,\qquad b=-2\pi\tau.
$$

Here a is phase at f0, b has units rad/Hz, and tau is the total differential
physical delay between the declared planes. The phase at f0 is an unknown nuisance
parameter: it is needed to describe the data even when delay is the desired result.
Let errors be independent centered Gaussian with known variance sigma² in rad²,
constant across these finite observations. Gaussian phase errors are a model,
justified only within the amplitude/SNR and unwrapping conditions discussed earlier.
A finite observation window, drift between frequency steps or correlated reference
errors can invalidate independence or the static response assumption.

An estimator is a rule taking data to a parameter estimate. Its bias is E[tauhat]-tau;
its variance measures scatter about its own mean; mean-square error equals variance
plus squared bias. These expectations refer to repetitions under the declared
model, not the scatter of one fitted residual sequence.

## Derive the fit from a likelihood

The likelihood treats the observed y as fixed and asks how its probability density
varies with the proposed a and b. For our Gaussian model its log, apart from a
parameter-independent constant, is

$$
 \ell(a,b)=-{1\over2\sigma^2}\sum_i(y_i-a-bx_i)^2.
$$

Maximizing this expression is equivalent to minimizing the residual sum of squares.
Differentiate with respect to a and b and set both derivatives to zero. Because
sum x_i=0, the two equations separate:

$$
 \widehat a=\bar y,\qquad
 \widehat b={\sum_i x_i y_i\over S_{xx}},\qquad
 S_{xx}=\sum_i x_i^2,\qquad
 \widehat\tau=-{\widehat b\over2\pi}.
$$

At least two distinct frequencies are necessary: Sxx=0 leaves slope unidentified.
These closed forms minimize the quadratic exactly. A zero derivative need not
identify a global maximum for an arbitrary nonlinear likelihood; here the positive
quadratic curvature supplies that conclusion. For known unequal variances, the
Gaussian log likelihood instead weights each squared residual by its inverse
variance. The mean frequency must then be weighted too. This precision weighting
and the hazards of estimated weights are discussed in the
[NIST regression handbook](https://itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pmd/section1/pmd143.htm).
For correlated data the quadratic is r^T C^{-1}r, with positive-definite known C;
whitening means applying a fixed transform W with WCW^T=I so transformed
errors have unit covariance. Its stable construction and coupled fitting are
extensions beyond this bounded scalar derivation. We do not assume that
relabeling samples makes their covariance diagonal.

Substituting the signal model into the fit shows its noise contribution directly:

$$
 \widehat b-b={\sum_i x_i\epsilon_i\over S_{xx}},\qquad
 \operatorname{var}\widehat\tau={\sigma^2\over4\pi^2 S_{xx}},\qquad
 \operatorname{var}\widehat a={\sigma^2\over N}.
$$

Both estimates are unbiased in this unwrapped linear model and their covariance
is zero because sum x_i=0. Changing the intercept reference to another frequency
changes its covariance with slope; it does not change the physical delay estimate.
The equations reveal the design lever: spread in observation frequency, not merely
sample count, controls local delay precision.

## What an information bound actually bounds

The score is the derivative of log likelihood. At the true parameters the slope
score is U_b=sum x_i epsilon_i/sigma². Its mean is zero and its second moment,
the Fisher information I_bb, is Sxx/sigma². The intercept score is
U_a=sum epsilon_i/sigma²; its cross moment with U_b vanishes. Centering frequencies
therefore separates nuisance intercept from slope information in this model.

Why does inverse information enter a bound? For an unbiased estimator of b,
differentiate its expectation with respect to b. If differentiation may pass
through the density integral, whose support does not depend on b, normalization
gives E[U_b]=0 and E[(bhat-b)U_b]=1. Cauchy–Schwarz then gives
var(bhat) E[U_b²] >= 1. Consequently

$$
 \operatorname{var}\widehat\tau\geq{\sigma^2\over4\pi^2 S_{xx}}.
$$

This is a local unbiased precision bound within a regular statistical model.
The linear Gaussian estimator above attains it: its error is a constant times the
score. Unknown correlated noise, parameter-dependent support, biased estimators,
branch selection and a wrong signal model require a different analysis. The
regularity and score framework is supported by MIT's
[lecture on efficient estimators](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/14-381-statistical-method-in-economics-fall-2018/15224973dfc1c2b4287804c8712681f7_MIT14_381F18_lec6.pdf),
§§2–3. A bound is not a guarantee that a practical acquisition algorithm finds
the correct solution. Its relevance must survive the ambiguity test below.

## Follow a consequential calculation

Use five synthetic offsets x_i=(-2,-1,0,1,2) MHz. Choose a=0.3 rad and tau=5 ns,
so b=-3.14159265e-8 rad/Hz. The noiseless phases are approximately
(0.362832, 0.331416, 0.300000, 0.268584, 0.237168) rad. They recover a and tau
by the formulas above. For assumed per-observation sigma=0.02 rad,
Sxx=1e13 Hz² and the predicted delay standard deviation is 1.00658 ns.
Intercept standard deviation is 0.00894427 rad. An illustrative requirement of
2 ns standard deviation is met locally. This is not a 2 ns total-error or accuracy
claim; it excludes unknown bias and global ambiguity.

If all offsets are halved, Sxx falls by four and delay standard deviation doubles
to 2.01317 ns, failing that illustrative local target. Repeating measurements at
the center frequency improves intercept estimation but contributes no centered
slope lever arm when the symmetric existing grid is retained. The receiver needs
band coverage, stability during the sweep and independent knowledge of nuisance
paths—not just a larger number of samples.

In @fig-delay-fit-precision the slope is negative for positive physical delay, and the frequency reference lies at the grid center. The hypothetical error bars describe individual phase errors, not total delay accuracy. Shrinking the frequency span leaves the five-sample count unchanged while degrading local precision.

![The declared five-frequency Gaussian phase model: noiseless central values, assumed individual one-standard-deviation bars, and local delay precision.](figures/delay-fit-precision.svg){#fig-delay-fit-precision fig-alt="A negative phase-frequency slope gives 5 ns total delay; halving the observation span doubles delay standard deviation and crosses the illustrative 2 ns target."}

## A precise local fit can be globally wrong

The actual complex observations are unchanged when each unwrapped phase changes
by an integer multiple of 2 pi. On a grid with spacing Delta_f, delays separated
by m/Delta_f give identical phasors after an appropriate intercept change. On our
centered integer grid, tau and tau+1 microsecond give exactly the same phasors
with the same a. Inferring 5 ns uniquely therefore needs prior range narrower
than an ambiguity interval with suitable boundary handling, or additional
noncommensurate frequencies or other observations. Additional frequencies only
help when their actual grid and precision distinguish the candidate delays.

Blindly unwrapping adjacent phases assumes that their true change is below pi
with enough noise margin; fades, gaps and low SNR can cause integer-cycle errors.
A small residual after selecting a branch does not prove that branch is right.
The Gaussian unwrapped likelihood above is not the exact likelihood of wrapped
noisy phasors through threshold failure. A practical search must retain plausible
branches and report ambiguity, rather than publish the local bound as total error.
A single tone cannot separate an arbitrary phase intercept from delay at all.

There is also a continuous identifiability failure. If an unknown receiver-path
delay d adds to the DUT delay, the phase slope is -2 pi(tau_DUT+d). Changing
(tau_DUT,d) to (tau_DUT+c,d-c) leaves every observation unchanged. No increase
in SNR or frequency span resolves that freedom. In our example an unmodeled
3 ns path would shift the fitted total from 5 ns to 8 ns without increasing the
linear residual. Referring the answer to DUT ports requires independent path
information and uncertainty; the calibration-specific procedure belongs later.

As a transfer problem, replace frequency offsets by centered observation times.
The same straight-line reasoning estimates a frequency offset from phase slope,
with slope +2 pi Delta_f rather than the physical-delay sign. Then add a quadratic
phase term q x_i²: its slope projection is Delta_b=q sum(x_i³)/Sxx, which can
vanish even on an asymmetric grid. The centered offsets (-8,-7,1,5,9) MHz
provide that counterexample. For a nonzero-bias example, center frequencies
(0,1,3) MHz: their third centered moment is nonzero. Calculate the projection
before claiming a delay bias. A residual check can reveal some curvature, but cannot detect a
perfectly linear unmodeled path. Distinguish precision, uniqueness and model truth
before using an inferred parameter to make a receiver decision.

The two slopes in @fig-delay-ambiguity coincide as wrapped phasors at every sampled frequency. Their off-grid predictions differ, but those predictions are not additional observations. Even a unique total slope would leave the DUT/receiver-delay split unresolved without independent path information.

![Delays 5 ns and 1005 ns on the centered 1 MHz grid. Gaps at principal-angle jumps avoid drawing them as continuous unwrapped transitions.](figures/delay-ambiguity.svg){#fig-delay-ambiguity fig-alt="Two different unwrapped slopes have identical wrapped samples at integer MHz offsets, while conditional off-grid predictions distinguish the branches."}

# Adequate calculations, models and uncertainty {#sec-model-adequacy}

An engineer can calculate a delay to many digits and still make the wrong receiver
decision. Numerical precision does not identify the physical delay, and a correct
uncertainty formula does not establish its input assumptions. We need a method
for deciding which approximation is adequate, which uncertainty matters, and what
evidence is missing before a result can support a design choice.

[Chapter 5](phase-delay-inference.qmd) supplies the inference example;
[Chapter 2](scalar-stochastic-phase.qmd) supplies scalar stochastic reasoning,
[Chapter 3](observation-weighted-coherence.qmd) supplies the Gaussian moments
and exponential-covariance average used below, and
[Chapter 4](covariance-quadratic-forms.qmd) supplies the covariance bridge. Here we assess a calculation built from those results rather than
create another competing phase or covariance convention. Positive physical delay
still gives negative input-oriented phase slope. Local envelope, phase and
spectral conventions remain local. The examples are synthetic teaching models,
not measurement uncertainty certificates or experimentally validated receivers.

## Start with a decision and its scales

Suppose two input-oriented phase observations at known physical frequencies
f1 and f2 are intended to estimate a total differential delay. Define
Delta_f=f2-f1>0 and dphi=phi2-phi1 on a justified unwrapped branch. A pure-delay
model with constant phase intercept gives

$$
 \tau=-{d\phi\over2\pi\Delta f}.
$$

The phase observations must already be translated through receiver conversion
orientation as explained in Chapter 5. Unknown receiver-path delay remains part
of the total; it does not vanish through this formula. We ask whether the model
can support an illustrative 0.15 ns standard-deviation target. That target is a
precision criterion, not a total-error or accuracy requirement.

Dimensional analysis checks the interface: radians divided by Hz yields seconds,
with the numerical 2 pi converting phase to cycles. Useful dimensionless scales
include phase error relative to one radian, frequency uncertainty relative to
Delta_f, and unmodeled phase curvature relative to fitted phase change. A small
parameter must control the neglected term, not merely be numerically small in
arbitrary units. For delay inference, even tiny voltage noise near an amplitude
null can give large phase error; voltage scale alone is the wrong criterion.

## Derive sensitivity and retain covariance

Let p be a vector of input quantities, p0 its nominal value and delta p a centered
small perturbation with covariance C_p. For the following quadratic-order
remainder, assume h is twice continuously differentiable with bounded second
derivatives throughout the relevant scaled input region. Taylor expansion gives

$$
 h(p_0+\delta p)=h(p_0)+g\,\delta p+O(\|\delta p\|^2),\qquad
 g_i={\partial h\over\partial p_i}\bigg|_{p_0}.
$$

The row g contains sensitivity coefficients. After declaring compatible coordinate
scales, its entries carry output units per input unit. Expanding the variance
of the first-order term yields

$$
 \operatorname{var}h\simeq g C_p g^T
 =\sum_i g_i^2 C_{ii}+2\sum_{i<j}g_i g_j C_{ij}.
$$

This is Chapter 4's quadratic form applied to the linearized output. It is exact
for an affine h, otherwise approximate. The first neglected mean correction is
one half the sum of Hessian entries H_ij=partial²h/(partial p_i partial p_j)
times C_ij, provided the second-order expansion has an integrable remainder
small relative to retained terms over the input distribution. For example, bounded
third derivatives throughout its support and a sufficiently small third absolute
perturbation moment control that remainder. Differentiability alone does not
justify a quadratic remainder: h(x)=|x|^(3/2) at zero has zero derivative but a
remainder larger than order x².
This warns that h(E[p]) need not equal E[h(p)]. Covariance-aware first-order
uncertainty propagation and inclusion of significant measurement-process inputs
are also specified in [NIST TN 1297, Appendix A.1–A.3](https://www.nist.gov/pml/nist-technical-note-1297/nist-tn-1297-appendix-law-propagation-uncertainty).
The theorem does not supply a missing physical input model.

A covariance may describe repeated receiver variability, uncertainty about a
fixed path parameter, or uncertainty of an estimator. These are different
ensembles or states of knowledge. Identify which is intended before combining
them. A confidence or coverage claim also requires distributional assumptions;
standard deviation alone does not specify a tail probability. A full measurement
uncertainty procedure and calibration evidence belong to later metrology work.

## Follow the delay budget through a changed assumption

Assume Delta_f=10 MHz and true total delay 5 ns. Then nominal dphi=-0.314159265 rad.
Let the centered phase errors be delta_phi1=u+e1 and delta_phi2=u+e2. The common
source u here is a frequency-independent phase-offset component common to
simultaneous multitone comparisons with identical normalized time weighting in
one fixed acquisition state. It is the same random draw in both observations,
not a universal oscillator timing-error model. Its variance is 0.00036 rad²; independent local terms e1,e2 each have variance
0.00004 rad² and are independent of u. Thus individual phase variances are
0.0004 rad², covariance is 0.00036 rad², and difference variance is 0.00008 rad².
This is a declared source/path construction, not a chosen correlation coefficient.

The phase sensitivities of tau are +1/(2 pi Delta_f) and -1/(2 pi Delta_f), so
the predicted delay standard deviation is

$$
 u_\tau={\sqrt{0.00008}\over2\pi\,10^7}\ {\rm s}
 =0.142353\ {\rm ns}.
$$

The illustrative precision target is met under the stated model. Incorrectly
treating the two phase errors as independent gives 0.450158 ns and would reject
the same design for the wrong reason. Conversely, deleting local noise because
the source is shared would be unjustified. Shared contributions cancel only
because their phase sensitivities and observation timing match in this model.
For sequential or differently filtered observations, replace u by distinct shared
source draws with equal variance V=0.00036 and correlation rho. Difference variance
then becomes 0.00008+2V(1-rho). The 0.15 ns target requires rho at least about
0.987741. This rho describes the shared-source draws, not the total phase errors.
Chapter 3 supplies the observation-dependent covariance calculation needed before
reusing that cancellation assumption.

For a concrete local input model, let Delta_f uncertainty be uniform on
[-sqrt(3)1000,+sqrt(3)1000] Hz about its 10 MHz nominal value, independent of
the phase inputs. Its standard uncertainty is 1000 Hz and its support stays far
from zero. Then its sensitivity is -tau/Delta_f. Its first-order contribution is
0.0005 ns standard uncertainty at the nominal point, negligible beside the phase
term here. That is a model-specific comparison. A frequency-scale bias or a
correlated phase/frequency error needs its own term and cannot be hidden inside
an independent variance. The reciprocal-frequency Taylor expansion is local. A small relative standard
uncertainty alone does not control rare near-zero gaps, where reciprocal moments
can become enormous or fail to exist. Justify support away from zero or adequate
tail/remainder control before treating the linearized variance as an adequate
output-uncertainty model; the bounded uniform model supplies that condition here.

Now change only the shared-source path: give channel 2 sensitivity 0.5 to u.
Difference variance becomes 0.25(0.00036)+0.00008=0.00017 rad², giving about
0.20751 ns standard deviation. The precision decision reverses. Neither more
digits in the solver nor a positive covariance matrix can rescue the original
conclusion after this physical assumption changes.

The two panels in @fig-uncertainty-sensitivity change different assumptions. The upper panel varies correlation between shared-source observations at fixed equal coupling; the lower keeps the same draw but changes its endpoint sensitivity. Either change can reverse the precision decision. These curves show the phase-derived uncertainty only; the separately declared bounded frequency-gap uncertainty contributes about 0.0005 ns at the nominal point.

![Phase-derived delay uncertainty for the supplied 10 MHz gap and source variances. The horizontal line is a standard-deviation criterion, not an accuracy or coverage bound.](figures/uncertainty-sensitivity.svg){#fig-uncertainty-sensitivity fig-alt="Delay uncertainty increases when shared-source draws decorrelate or their path sensitivities differ; common cancellation meets the target only under closely matched observation conditions."}

## A zero derivative does not mean zero uncertainty

Consider a normalized quadrature observation y=sin(phi) near phi=pi/2. Write
phi=pi/2+delta with delta centered Gaussian of variance sigma²; then y=cos(delta).
The derivative with respect to delta at zero vanishes, so first-order propagation
predicts zero variance. The prediction is inadequate, not evidence of a noiseless
observation. The expansion y≈1-delta²/2 instead gives a mean shift -sigma²/2
and variance sigma^4/2, using the Gaussian fourth moment developed in Chapter 3.

There is an independent exact check. Chapter 3's Gaussian characteristic function
gives E[cos(delta)]=exp(-sigma²/2). The identity cos²(delta)=(1+cos(2delta))/2
then gives

$$
 E[y]=e^{-\sigma^2/2},\qquad
 \operatorname{var}y={1\over2}(1-e^{-\sigma^2})^2.
$$

At sigma=0.2 rad, the exact mean is 0.980199 and standard deviation is 0.0277261;
the second-order approximation gives 0.0282843. An illustrative y-standard-deviation
limit of 0.01 fails despite the first-order zero. Moreover y cannot distinguish
+delta from -delta. Inverting near this maximum introduces branch ambiguity and
large sensitivity; a small output change cannot be interpreted as a unique phase
change. Nonlinear propagation, a distribution or interval calculation, and the
actual identifiable observable must replace an invalid first-order result.

The tangent in @fig-nonlinear-uncertainty is flat, but the actual response changes on both sides of its maximum. The lower panel shows why propagating only that tangent misses both the uncertainty and the two-branch interpretation of the inverse.

![Exact and local cosine models, followed by output standard deviation under the declared Gaussian phase model. The output and its uncertainty are dimensionless.](figures/nonlinear-uncertainty.svg){#fig-nonlinear-uncertainty fig-alt="A flat first-order tangent predicts zero uncertainty while the exact and second-order calculations give nonzero output scatter and preserve the symmetry between positive and negative phase deviations."}

## Numerical agreement must be about distinct formulations

The finite-average variance for exponential phase covariance in Chapter 3 contains
the dimensionless factor

$$
 g(x)={2(x-1+e^{-x})\over x^2},\qquad x=T/t_c>0.
$$

This is a numerical evaluation example of that existing result, not a new canonical
derivation. Its physical limit as x tends to zero is one: the phase is nearly
constant within a short observation. Direct floating-point subtraction at x=1e-8
can produce g≈2.220446 on the tested Python environment. It subtracts nearly equal
numbers and then divides the rounding error by x². More printed digits do not help.

Expand exp(-x) before subtracting: g=1-x/3+x²/12-x³/60+..., giving approximately
0.999999996667 at that x. A distinct time-domain check is
2 integral_0^1 (1-v)exp(-xv) dv. It avoids the cancellation and can be quadratured
with resolution refinement. A converged integral and a stable series test numerical
consistency; they do not prove that an actual receiver has exponential covariance.

Specify numerical error relative to the decision margin. Refine integration step
or spectral cutoff, inspect changes and bound a neglected tail where possible.
Step refinement alone can miss oscillatory structure if both grids undersample it;
a shared formula in two programs can preserve the same sign error. Compare a
different formulation, asymmetry, units and limits before interpreting agreement.
For the inference and tracking examples, use source sums versus covariance, time
integration versus transfer response, and known ambiguity cases as separate checks.

The error curves in @fig-numerical-cancellation compare binary64 evaluations with a 65-digit reference at the same input values. The series preserves the short-observation limit; direct subtraction can fail badly even though the physical model is unchanged. Values outside the plotted relative-error range, including errors below its lower limit, are omitted rather than assigned a fabricated floor.

![Illustrative floating-point evaluation errors on the tested Python environment. Independent time-domain integration is the separate consistency check; neither calculation validates receiver physics.](figures/numerical-cancellation.svg){#fig-numerical-cancellation fig-alt="Direct subtraction loses accuracy at short observation ratios, while the local series remains close to a high-precision reference."}

## Choose the smallest model that preserves the decision

Separate four questions in the report: encoded mathematical correctness, numerical
error, input uncertainty and model discrepancy. Model discrepancy is the difference
between the chosen physical representation and the relevant actual behavior at
specified inputs and states. It is not automatically an independent random noise
term. Without physical evidence its magnitude may remain unknown.

A pure-delay model may be enough for an introductory local fit. Frequency-dependent
path response, asynchronous sampling or drift during a sweep may require a richer
model. An unmodeled 0.5 ns receiver path would bias a DUT-referred result by 0.5 ns
while preserving a perfectly linear phase slope. Passing the 0.15 ns precision
target does not bound that bias. Calibration or independent path evidence is needed
before claiming DUT accuracy. Computational refinement cannot provide it.

For a transfer assessment, halve Delta_f without changing the declared phase
covariance: delay standard deviation doubles, reversing the nominal precision
decision. Then retain Delta_f but change the common-source coupling as above;
reconstruct C_p before propagating it. Finally compare a desired slow phase
variation in a tracking residual with the same variation in the correction output
in [Chapter 7](tracking-signal-retention.qmd). A quieter output can represent
signal suppression rather than a more accurate physical model. Adequacy is judged
against the observable and decision, with unsupported extrapolations left explicit.
